justification_text:
My point estimates reflect a gradual upward drift across the three horizons, starting near 89.5 for the one-day forecast, rising to 90.5 at one week, and reaching 92.0 at one month. This mild positive slope likely stems from an assumption of modest underlying momentum or mean-reversion toward a slightly higher equilibrium level, combined with whatever near-term trend was visible in the data at the time of the forecast. The one-day estimate is anchored most heavily to the last observed value, with only a small expected move, while the one-week and one-month estimates incorporate a gentle drift that reflects either a trend extrapolation or a structural view that the series tends to edge higher over time.

The confidence interval widths widen substantially as the horizon extends, which is the standard consequence of uncertainty compounding over time. At one day, the 90% interval spans only 7 points, reflecting relatively low short-run volatility and the high predictability of the next single observation given recent history. At one week the interval expands to 15 points, and by one month it reaches 32 points, acknowledging that cumulative shocks, regime shifts, and changing conditions can push the outcome meaningfully away from the central path. The widening also reflects the growing relevance of macro or structural factors that are hard to pin down at longer horizons.

Several specific risks could push outcomes outside these stated intervals. On the downside, a sudden negative shock — such as a policy change, a deteriorating macroeconomic print, or a liquidity event — could drive the series well below 86 even within the first day, let alone over a month. On the upside, a strong positive catalyst or a short-covering rally could push values above 108 at the one-month horizon if momentum accelerates beyond what the baseline drift assumes. The stated intervals represent the range I assigned a combined 90% probability to, meaning I implicitly accepted roughly a 5% chance of outcomes on each tail being more extreme than shown.

It is also worth acknowledging that the interval construction depends on assumptions about the distributional shape of future outcomes, likely something close to normally distributed residuals around the trend. If the true distribution has fat tails — which financial and economic series often do — the stated intervals may be too narrow even if the point estimates are reasonable. Structural breaks, correlated shocks, or non-linear feedback dynamics are all mechanisms that could produce tail outcomes more frequently than the symmetric, gradually widening bands would suggest.
